units.title: Identity

listening1.stem: Which project shows how Mariam wants to introduce herself?
listening1.script: Mariam is preparing a display for visitors who have never met her. She wants them to see her photograph with short notes about what she likes and what she does well. A family tree would show her relatives, and a map would show her neighbourhood. Neither would tell visitors enough about her own interests.

listening1.stem: Which hobby is Layla most interested in?
listening1.script: Layla is confident but rather quiet in large groups. Her brother plays football and her cousin enjoys photography. Layla, however, is brilliant at drawing, and she is spending this month learning how to use watercolours. Her family is buying her an art palette for the exhibition.

listening1.stem: Which picture best shows Rashid's usual behaviour with new classmates?
listening1.script: Rashid enjoys meeting people. When someone new joins the class, he usually waves, walks over and introduces himself. His brother prefers reading on his own, and his cousin often feels too nervous to enter a room full of strangers. Rashid is the one who makes new pupils feel welcome.

listening1.stem: Which family tradition is Salma learning?
listening1.script: Salma comes from a family that enjoys making things by hand. Her uncle plays the oud and her cousin makes pots from clay. Salma is learning from her grandmother to fold strips of palm leaf over and under one another. She hopes to make a small basket for their next family gathering.

listening1.stem: Which family activity does Rana usually enjoy at weekends?
listening1.script: Rana says her family sometimes visits the beach and occasionally goes shopping. They usually prefer spending a night outdoors, however, because everyone enjoys talking beneath the stars. They are preparing their tents for this weekend, so camping is the activity she describes in her personal profile.

interview: Interviewer
Welcome to our school identity programme. What encouraged you to make a personal photo board, Huda?
Huda
I noticed that classmates who seemed different often shared hobbies, so I wanted to help people discover them.
Interviewer
Did the first display focus only on people's appearance, or did you include their interests as well?
Huda
We included their hobbies, family traditions and personal strengths. Appearance cannot explain the whole story of someone's identity.
Interviewer
Where did your team first collect information for the project, and how did you ask pupils to contribute?
Huda
We visited three classes and offered simple questionnaires. Everyone was free to answer privately or leave a question blank.
Interviewer
When did you begin preparing the photographs, and how long did your work take altogether?
Huda
We started in October and worked for nearly three weeks before the first display was ready.
Interviewer
Who helped you organise the captions, and which languages did you decide to use?
Huda
Our English teacher helped us. We wrote short captions in both Arabic and English so more families could understand.
Interviewer
What happened when one classmate changed her mind about showing a photograph? Did this cause an argument?
Huda
No. We removed her picture immediately and used a drawing instead. Respecting someone's choice matters more than a display.
Interviewer
How did the project change the way students talked to one another at school?
Huda
People began asking about interests rather than making quick assumptions. Several shy pupils also joined clubs that suited them.
interviewQs: Why did Huda want to make a personal photo board?
To show that different classmates shared hobbies
To choose a winner for a photo competition
To advertise a new sports centre
What did the display include besides photographs?
Timetables and examination results
Hobbies, family traditions and personal strengths
Mainly descriptions of classmates' appearance
How did the pupils collect information?
They offered questionnaires pupils could answer privately
They asked everyone to speak in front of the school
They looked up pupils’ interests on the internet
Why were the captions written in Arabic and English?
To practise reading aloud in both languages
To make them easier for more families to understand
To make the captions longer
What did the group do when a pupil changed her mind about a photograph?
They kept her photograph on display
They moved her photograph to another room
They used a drawing in its place
matchPeople: Hamad enjoys designing posters that express his personality through colours, shapes and drawings. He wants to practise creative techniques.
Salma has moved to a new town and wants to learn about classmates' family traditions and the stories behind them.
Rashid is shy when speaking to strangers but enjoys astronomy and hopes to meet others who share this interest.
Amal enjoys sport and wants to work with a small team while improving her football skills.
matchOptions: A: Meet a group of young astronomers who explore the night sky and share discoveries through short presentations.
B: Learn to paint and design personal posters that show your ideas, interests and individual style.
C: Join a football team that welcomes new players and values teamwork, respect and regular practice.
D: Listen to students share family traditions and create a short bilingual collection of personal memories.
E: Compete in an advanced mathematics competition with no preparation sessions.
reading2Questions: What subject does Aisha enjoy studying in the evening?
Which artistic task did Salma volunteer to do?
Who felt confident speaking to visitors?
Which pupil preferred organising details quietly?
Name one feature Aisha now includes in the meaning of identity.
What skill is Aisha learning when she listens first?
units.writing1: Write a story about joining a new class and discovering that one of your classmates shares an unexpected interest with you. Describe how you felt at first, what happened and how the friendship developed. Write at least 100 words.
units.writing2: Write an email to a new school friend introducing your hobbies, personality, family traditions and the activities you are enjoying this month. Use present simple and present continuous appropriately. Write at least 100 words.

units.title: Connections

listening1.stem: How did the students speak to their partner class?
listening1.script: Our class wanted to ask students in another town about the expressions they use at home. A letter would take several days, and our partner class could not travel to see us. We were able to see their faces on the screen and ask them questions straight away while the call was running.

listening1.stem: Which device did the team use to keep a record of the interview?
listening1.script: We wanted to capture our grandparents’ voices and the gestures they made as they spoke. A handheld recorder could only save the sound, and our phone was almost out of power. In the end we put the device on a tripod and used its top microphone to capture both the picture and the sound.

listening1.stem: How did the visitor communicate with the students?
listening1.script: The visitor showed us that you can have a conversation without speaking. She did not point to pictures on a board and she did not speak into a microphone. Instead, she made different movements with her hands while using her face to show how she felt. We tried to reply in the same way.

listening1.stem: What were the pupils recording for their language project?
listening1.script: Some pupils thought the project would involve reading quietly or typing examples from a book. Our teacher wanted to collect language as people really use it. So I sat with my grandmother and listened as she told me about her childhood in the village. I recorded her voice with her permission.

listening1.stem: What helped Hana understand the visitor's message?
listening1.script: At the exhibition, a visitor showed Hana a short message in a language she was still learning. Hana could not find the right page in the leaflet, and she did not need to call anybody. She opened a tool on her phone, chose both languages and showed the visitor the new version of the message.

interview: Interviewer
Today we are discussing how young people can protect languages and share stories. Why did your class begin this project, Bilal?
Bilal
We realised that some children understood their grandparents' words but rarely tried speaking the same language themselves.
Interviewer
Were you studying only written words, or were you interested in conversations and stories as well?
Bilal
We focused on conversations. A language lives through the people who use it and tell stories in it.
Interviewer
Where did your first interview take place, and who was the guest that day?
Bilal
We recorded our first interview at the community centre with my grandmother, who loves telling family stories.
Interviewer
What happened while you were checking the recording, and how did your team respond to the problem?
Bilal
The microphone stopped working for a few minutes. We checked the batteries and repeated that section patiently.
Interviewer
What language did the grandparents speak during the interview? Did you translate anything for younger students?
Bilal
They spoke Arabic, and two pupils added short English summaries so the whole class could learn from them.
Interviewer
When did you share the collection, and how did you protect personal information in the recordings?
Bilal
We shared it on Tuesday during the school exhibition, but we used only recordings that families had approved.
Interviewer
What was the most important lesson you learned about communication through this project?
Bilal
Listening respectfully is as important as speaking clearly. We should ask questions instead of pretending we understand.
interviewQs: Why did Bilal's class start the project?
Some children understood their grandparents' language but rarely spoke it
The school needed more textbook recordings
Families had asked for a reading competition
What type of language did the pupils focus on?
Written notices
Conversations and stories
Formal speeches
How did the team deal with a problem during the interview?
They replaced the guest
They wrote out the answers from memory
They checked the batteries and repeated part of the interview
Why did two pupils add short English summaries?
So the whole class could learn from the recordings
So the guest could read the questions in advance
So they could shorten the interview itself
How did the team protect the families’ privacy?
They removed everyone’s voice from the recordings
They shared only recordings approved by the families
They posted the interviews without asking
matchPeople: Maryam would like to interview elderly relatives about the words and expressions they used when they were younger.
Salim finds English pronunciation difficult and wants patient practice speaking and listening.
Nasser wants to learn how cameras and microphones capture conversations without losing the speaker's meaning.
Fatma has prepared a bilingual project and needs advice on expressing the same idea clearly in different languages.
matchOptions: A: Audio skills club: learn to record, edit and check interviews without changing what speakers meant.
B: Pronunciation circle: practise listening carefully and saying unfamiliar words with friendly feedback.
C: Family memories: plan respectful questions and record older relatives telling stories about the past.
D: Translation workshop: compare messages in two languages and learn how to explain a meaning accurately.
E: Weekend mountain climbing for athletes with advanced equipment.
reading2Questions: What did Mariam's class make about communication?
Who did the class interview about earlier ways of sharing news?
What seemed to disappear from the shared folder?
Who had moved the missing recording?
What did the team agree to record in future?
units.writing1: Write a story about a message that caused a misunderstanding while you were preparing a school event. Use past simple and past continuous, include a clear solution and write at least 100 words.
units.writing2: Write an email to a friend describing a language or communication project in which you took part. Explain what you learned about listening, speaking, translation or technology. Write at least 100 words.

units.title: The future is now

listening1.stem: Which invention will carry supplies across the valley?
listening1.script: The village team wants to deliver small parcels after heavy rain closes the road. A driverless car still needs a road, and a wheeled robot cannot cross the flooded path. The engineers are going to try a device with four rotors. It will lift each parcel into the air and carry it across the valley.

listening1.stem: Which system will Ali use to check whether plants are healthy?
listening1.script: Ali is developing a useful tool for people who grow vegetables at home. It will not water the plants or switch their lights on. A device will take a close picture of each leaf and send it to a computer. The program will compare the picture with examples of healthy and unhealthy leaves.

listening1.stem: Which smart-home device will help the family save energy?
listening1.script: The family is testing a new way to use less electricity at home. They considered a smart speaker and a robot vacuum, but neither manages the heating. Their new device will measure the temperature in the room and turn the heating down automatically when everyone leaves the house.

listening1.stem: What kind of robot is the team going to build?
listening1.script: Our team is going to make a robot that collects empty bottles outside. A fixed arm could reach only one spot, and a robot that walks would be difficult to build. We chose a low machine with four wheels that can travel along a path and use a claw to pick up litter.

listening1.stem: Which device can check the wearer's skin temperature?
listening1.script: The health club is testing three types of technology. A phone can show a report and an earbud can play a reminder, but neither will touch the skin on the wrist. The device we will test has a strap and a small screen. Its sensor can check the temperature at the wrist.

interview: Interviewer
Welcome to Future Voices. What kind of technology is your science club developing, Noura, and who might benefit from it?
Noura
We are building a simple device that reminds older people to drink water at regular times during the day.
Interviewer
Did the idea come from a famous inventor, or did someone in your local community suggest it?
Noura
My grandmother suggested it when she forgot to drink enough water during a busy afternoon last year.
Interviewer
How will the device work, and does it use artificial intelligence to make medical decisions for its user?
Noura
A timer activates a small light and a sound. It never gives medical advice; people still make their own decisions.
Interviewer
Where are the students going to test the prototype, and who is supervising the trial?
Noura
We are going to test it in the science laboratory next month with our teacher and a volunteer engineer.
Interviewer
What happened when you tried an early version, and how are you changing the design because of that problem?
Noura
The warning was too quiet, so we are adding a brighter signal as well as a clearer button.
Interviewer
When is your team meeting the engineer again? Is the appointment already confirmed with the school?
Noura
We are meeting her on Wednesday. The school timetable confirms that she will arrive before the second break.
Interviewer
What advice would you give other students who want to design useful technology for families?
Noura
Ask people what they need, test your ideas carefully and remember that technology should support human judgement.
interviewQs: What is the science club’s device designed to do?
Check how much exercise people get
Remind older people to drink water
Measure the temperature of a drink
How does the device tell someone it is time to drink?
A timer switches on a light and a sound
A phone sends a written reminder
A sensor shakes the water bottle
How does the team plan to test the prototype?
At home without collecting feedback
At a sports centre with an older student
In the science lab with a teacher and an engineer
What problem did the first version have?
The light stayed on all day
It was too difficult to carry
The sound was too quiet
What does Noura recommend before designing technology for families?
Ask people about their needs and test ideas carefully
Add more features before talking to anyone
Let the device make all the decisions
matchPeople: Amal is designing a reminder system and wants to learn how safe technology can assist older relatives at home.
Rashid wants to understand how computer programs recognise patterns in photographs without replacing human decisions.
Huda enjoys filming and hopes to create interactive entertainment that responds to the viewer's choices.
Salim wants to predict his team's performance by using sensor readings collected during running practice.
matchOptions: A: Interactive media club: explore how a story or film can change in response to what an audience chooses.
B: Health design workshop: create and test simple reminder devices that support people's everyday routines.
C: Image technology group: learn how software identifies patterns and why humans must verify results.
D: Sports technology workshop: compare distance and movement information from safe wearable sensors.
E: A historical costume workshop about traditional clothing from previous centuries.

units.writing2: Write an email to your science teacher proposing an invention that helps people with technology. Explain how it will work, when you are going to test it and what advice you need. Write at least 100 words.
